mechanical-001.question: Which statement about the Young's modulus of steel is correct?
choices: When quenching or cold working doubles the strength, the Young's modulus also becomes roughly twice as large
It is determined by the strength of interatomic bonding and changes little with heat treatment or working
It is the yield stress divided by the total strain up to yielding, and represents the slope of the plastic region
mechanical-001.explanation: Young's modulus is the ratio of stress to strain in the elastic region, E = σ/ε. It is set by the strength of interatomic bonding (the curvature of the interatomic potential) and is a structure-insensitive property. That is why it stays at around 200 GPa whether the steel is mild or quenched, and doubling the strength does not double the modulus. Yield strength and hardness are structure-sensitive properties governed by how easily dislocations move, and they change greatly with heat treatment and working. Young's modulus is the slope of the straight elastic line, distinct from the slope of the plastic region (the work-hardening rate). As temperature rises, bonding weakens and the modulus decreases gradually.

mechanical-002.question: A round bar 10 mm in diameter carries a tensile load of 10 kN. Which value is closest to the engineering stress?
choices: About 31.8 MPa
About 127 MPa
About 0.127 MPa
mechanical-002.explanation: The cross-sectional area is A = πd²/4 = π × (10 mm)²/4 ≈ 78.5 mm², so the engineering stress is σ = F/A = 10000 N / 78.5 mm² ≈ 127 N/mm² = 127 MPa (1 N/mm² = 1 MPa). About 31.8 MPa comes from mistaking the diameter for the radius and taking A = π × (10 mm)² ≈ 314 mm². About 0.127 MPa results from the wrong area conversion 1 mm² = 10⁻³ m²; the correct one is 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m². Engineering stress is based on the original cross-sectional area, so it differs from the actual stress after necking begins.

mechanical-003.question: A steel rod 2.0 m long with a Young's modulus of 200 GPa is loaded in tension to 100 MPa within its elastic range. Which value is closest to the elongation of the rod?
choices: About 0.10 mm
About 1.0 mm
About 10 mm
mechanical-003.explanation: From Hooke's law, the strain is ε = σ/E = 100×10⁶ / (200×10⁹) = 5.0×10⁻⁴. The elongation is ΔL = εL = 5.0×10⁻⁴ × 2000 mm = 1.0 mm. About 0.10 mm and about 10 mm are off by one order of magnitude from a slip in the GPa–MPa conversion (1 GPa = 1000 MPa) or the m–mm conversion. Even in a steel with a yield stress of several hundred MPa, the elastic strain stays at only about 0.1–0.2%. At the same stress, an aluminum alloy with about one third the modulus (about 70 GPa) stretches about three times as much, a difference that matters in stiffness-critical design.

mechanical-004.question: For materials such as aluminum alloys that show no distinct yield point, which correctly describes how the 0.2% offset yield strength is determined?
choices: Read the stress on the stress–strain curve directly at the point where the strain is 0.2%
Take the stress where a line parallel to the elastic line, offset by a strain of 0.2%, intersects the stress–strain curve
Take the stress equal to 0.2% of the tensile strength obtained from the maximum load
mechanical-004.explanation: The 0.2% offset yield strength is defined as the stress that leaves a permanent (plastic) strain of 0.2% when the load is removed. On the stress–strain curve, shift the elastic line by 0.002 along the strain axis and read the stress where it meets the curve. Reading the stress at a strain of 0.2% directly differs from the definition because that strain includes elastic strain, and it gives a lower value. The maximum load corresponds to the tensile strength, a different quantity from the offset yield strength. For materials such as mild steel that show distinct upper and lower yield points, the yield point value is used.

mechanical-005.question: In a tensile test, the engineering stress was 400 MPa at an engineering strain of 0.20, before necking began. Assuming constant volume during plastic deformation, which value is closest to the true stress at this point?
choices: About 333 MPa
About 400 MPa
About 480 MPa
mechanical-005.explanation: Constant volume gives A₀L₀ = AL, so A = A₀/(1 + e), and the true stress is σ_T = σ(1 + e) = 400 × 1.20 = 480 MPa. The true strain at this point is ε_T = ln(1 + e) = ln 1.20 ≈ 0.182. About 333 MPa divides by (1 + e) where it should multiply; as the cross section shrinks, the actual stress becomes larger than the engineering stress. About 400 MPa is just the engineering stress, ignoring the reduction in area. This conversion is valid only up to the onset of necking, while deformation is uniform throughout the specimen.

mechanical-006.question: Which statement about the Vickers hardness test is correct?
choices: A diamond square pyramid indenter with a 136° angle between opposite faces is pressed in, and hardness is found from the indentation diagonals
A cemented carbide or steel ball, for example 10 mm in diameter, is pressed in, and hardness is found from the indentation diameter
Hardness is found from the difference in depth of a diamond cone or similar indenter under a minor and a major load, without measuring the indentation size
mechanical-006.explanation: In the Vickers test, a square-based diamond pyramid indenter with a 136° angle between opposite faces is pressed in, the surface area is found from the mean length d of the two diagonals of the indentation, and HV = 0.1891F/d² (F in N, d in mm). Because the indenter shapes are geometrically similar, the value stays nearly constant as the load changes, which suits measurements on thin layers and small regions (microhardness testing). Pressing in a ball and measuring the indentation diameter is the Brinell test, suited to measuring the average hardness of coarse microstructures. Using the difference in indentation depth is the Rockwell test, convenient for inspecting mass-produced parts. Conversions between test methods are empirical.

mechanical-007.question: A steel plate with a fracture toughness K_IC = 50 MPa·√m carries a tensile stress of 200 MPa. Using K = Yσ√(πa) with a geometry factor Y = 1.0, which value is closest to the critical crack length a at which fracture occurs?
choices: About 20 mm
About 62.5 mm
About 80 mm
mechanical-007.explanation: Setting K = K_IC gives a = (1/π)(K_IC/Yσ)². K_IC/σ = 50/200 = 0.25 √m, so a = 0.25²/π = 0.0625/3.14 ≈ 0.0199 m, about 20 mm. About 62.5 mm forgets to divide by π, and about 80 mm is the mistake of taking 0.25/π without squaring. The critical crack length is inversely proportional to the square of the stress, so halving the stress allows a crack four times as long. Comparing the crack sizes that nondestructive inspection can detect against this critical value is the basis of damage-tolerant design.

mechanical-008.question: When the fracture toughness of plates of the same material but different thickness is measured, what happens to the apparent fracture toughness K_c as the thickness increases?
choices: It keeps increasing, since thicker plates have larger plastic zones
It is a material constant, so it is the same for any thickness
It decreases as constraint grows, approaching the plane-strain value K_IC
mechanical-008.explanation: In a thin plate, constraint through the thickness is weak (close to plane stress), so the plastic zone at the crack tip spreads widely and absorbs much energy, giving a high apparent fracture toughness K_c. As the plate thickens, deformation through the thickness is constrained and the plate approaches plane strain; the plastic zone shrinks and K_c decreases, leveling off above a certain thickness at a nearly constant minimum, K_IC. This is why K_IC can be treated as a material constant and is used in design as a conservative value. Test standards require a thickness, proportional to (K_IC/yield stress)², large enough for plane strain to hold.

mechanical-009.question: Which statement about fatigue S-N curves is correct?
choices: Carbon steels often show a fatigue limit, a stress amplitude below which they rarely fail however many cycles are applied
Aluminum alloys show a more distinct fatigue limit than carbon steels, with the S-N curve becoming fully flat from around 10⁶ cycles
A larger tensile mean stress keeps cracks from opening and slows their growth, so the fatigue life at the same stress amplitude is longer
mechanical-009.explanation: For carbon and low-alloy steels, the S-N curve often flattens out at around 10⁶–10⁷ cycles, showing a fatigue limit below which failure becomes unlikely. FCC metals such as aluminum and copper alloys rarely show a distinct flat portion, so they are rated by the strength at a set number of cycles such as 10⁷ (the fatigue strength). A tensile mean stress acts to open cracks and speeds their growth, so the life is shorter at the same stress amplitude, and corrections are made with tools such as the Goodman diagram. Note that in corrosive environments or in the very-high-cycle regime beyond 10⁸ cycles, even steels may not show a clear fatigue limit.

mechanical-010.question: What is the stress amplitude of a cyclic stress with a maximum of +300 MPa and a minimum of −100 MPa?
choices: 100 MPa
400 MPa
200 MPa
mechanical-010.explanation: The stress amplitude is σa = (σmax − σmin)/2 = (300 − (−100))/2 = 200 MPa. The mean stress is σm = (σmax + σmin)/2 = (300 + (−100))/2 = 100 MPa, and the stress ratio is R = σmin/σmax = −100/300 ≈ −0.33. 100 MPa is the mean stress, and 400 MPa is the stress range Δσ, the difference between maximum and minimum. Stress amplitude and stress range differ by a factor of two, so always check which one a data sheet or standard is quoting. Fully reversed loading with zero mean stress (R = −1) is the basic condition for fatigue testing.

mechanical-011.question: Take about 0.4 times the melting point (in absolute temperature) as the rough temperature above which creep can no longer be ignored. For aluminum (melting point 660 °C), which value is closest to this temperature?
choices: About 100 °C
About 264 °C
About 373 °C
mechanical-011.explanation: This rule of thumb works in absolute temperature, so with Tm = 660 + 273 = 933 K, 0.4Tm ≈ 373 K, about 100 °C. About 264 °C is the mistake of computing 0.4 × 660 in °C, and about 373 °C mistakes 373 K for °C. This ratio (the homologous temperature) varies between materials, roughly 0.3–0.5, but for aluminum alloys creep and loss of strength must be considered from about 100 °C upward, and low-melting solders creep even at room temperature. Creep proceeds through three stages, primary, secondary (steady-state) and tertiary, before rupture, and the steady-state creep rate is the key quantity in design.

mechanical-012.question: Which material shows a distinct ductile-to-brittle transition at low temperatures?
choices: Austenitic stainless steel (FCC)
Aluminum alloys (FCC)
Ferritic carbon steel (BCC)
mechanical-012.explanation: In BCC metals, the stress needed to move dislocations (the Peierls stress) rises sharply as temperature falls, so at low temperatures cleavage fracture occurs before yielding and the absorbed energy in the Charpy impact test drops abruptly over a certain temperature range. This is the ductile-to-brittle transition, and ferritic carbon steel is the classic example. FCC austenitic stainless steels and aluminum alloys have many slip systems and dislocations remain mobile at low temperatures, so they show no distinct transition and are used for cryogenic applications such as liquefied gas tanks. The transition temperature is lowered by grain refinement and raised by neutron irradiation and similar damage.

mechanical-013.question: A steel round bar 10 mm in diameter is loaded elastically with a tensile stress of 200 MPa. Taking Young's modulus as 200 GPa and Poisson's ratio as 0.30, which is closest to the change in diameter?
choices: Decreases by about 3.0 µm
Increases by about 3.0 µm
Decreases by about 10 µm
mechanical-013.explanation: The axial strain is ε = σ/E = 200×10⁶/(200×10⁹) = 1.0×10⁻³. Poisson's ratio is the negative ratio of lateral to axial strain, ν = −ε_lateral/ε_axial, so the lateral strain is −0.30 × 1.0×10⁻³ = −3.0×10⁻⁴. The change in diameter is −3.0×10⁻⁴ × 10 mm = −3.0×10⁻³ mm, a decrease of about 3.0 µm. A bar becomes thinner in tension, so the statement that it increases has the sign reversed. A decrease of about 10 µm applies the axial strain directly to the diameter without multiplying by Poisson's ratio. Most metals have a Poisson's ratio around 0.3; 0.5 is the upper limit, corresponding to no change in volume.

mechanical-014.question: A metal whose true stress σ and true strain ε are related by σ = Kεⁿ is pulled in tension. If necking (localized contraction) begins when dσ/dε = σ (Considère's criterion), at what true strain does necking begin?
choices: ε = 1/n
ε = n
ε = K·n
mechanical-014.explanation: Differentiating σ = Kεⁿ gives dσ/dε = nKεⁿ⁻¹. Setting this equal to σ = Kεⁿ gives nKεⁿ⁻¹ = Kεⁿ, and dividing both sides by Kεⁿ⁻¹ gives ε = n. The true strain of uniform elongation up to necking thus equals the strain-hardening exponent n. Necking begins when the loss of load-bearing capacity from the shrinking cross section outweighs the strengthening from work hardening; on the engineering stress-strain curve, this point is the tensile strength. Materials with a larger n elongate more uniformly and suit forming such as deep drawing. ε = 1/n solves the condition the wrong way round, and ε = K·n does not even have consistent dimensions.

mechanical-015.question: Which statement about resilience and toughness, obtained from a tensile stress-strain curve, is correct?
choices: Resilience is the total area under the curve up to fracture and toughness is the area under the elastic region, both set by strength alone
Both are set by the tensile strength alone and are unrelated to elongation, so a stronger material always has greater toughness
Resilience is the area under the elastic region, about σy²/(2E), and toughness is the total area under the curve up to fracture
mechanical-015.explanation: Resilience is the elastic energy stored per unit volume up to yielding, the area of the triangle under the elastic line, σy²/(2E). It is energy recovered on unloading and matters for spring materials. Toughness is the energy absorbed per unit volume up to fracture, the total area under the curve. Both have units of J/m³. Toughness depends on both strength and ductility, so a strong material with little elongation has low toughness, and a somewhat weaker material that elongates a lot may be tougher. The statement swapping the total area and the elastic area, and the statement that elongation does not matter, are wrong.

mechanical-016.question: Which is closest to the shear modulus G of an isotropic steel with a Young's modulus of 200 GPa and a Poisson's ratio of 0.30?
choices: About 77 GPa
About 154 GPa
About 167 GPa
mechanical-016.explanation: An isotropic elastic solid has only two independent elastic constants, and the shear modulus is G = E/[2(1 + ν)]. G = 200/(2 × 1.30) ≈ 76.9 GPa, about 77 GPa. About 154 GPa drops the factor 2 in the denominator, and about 167 GPa is the bulk modulus K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)], confused with the shear modulus. The shear modulus expresses resistance to shear and torsion and is used to calculate the twist of shafts, the energy of dislocations and estimates of the theoretical shear strength. For strongly anisotropic materials such as single crystals, this relation does not hold as it stands.

mechanical-017.question: A round bar is pulled with an axial tensile stress σ. Which combination gives the plane on which the largest shear stress acts and its magnitude?
choices: The cross section normal to the axis, with magnitude σ
Planes inclined at 45° to the axis, with magnitude σ/√2
Planes inclined at 45° to the axis, with magnitude σ/2
mechanical-017.explanation: On a plane whose normal makes an angle φ with the axis, the area grows to A/cosφ and the force component along the plane is F sinφ, so the shear stress is τ = σ sinφ cosφ = (σ/2) sin 2φ. Its maximum, σ/2, occurs at φ = 45°. σ/√2 resolves the force but forgets that the area also grows. The cross section normal to the axis carries only the normal stress σ and no shear stress. The roughly 45° inclination of slip in ductile metals and of the shear lip at the rim of a cup-and-cone fracture corresponds to this direction of maximum shear stress.

mechanical-018.question: Which statement about the change in volume when a metal bar is pulled in tension is correct?
choices: In elastic deformation the volume increases slightly because Poisson's ratio is below 0.5, while in plastic deformation the volume stays nearly constant
In both elastic and plastic deformation the lateral contraction cancels the extension, so the volume always stays exactly constant
In elastic deformation the volume is constant, but in plastic deformation the growing number of dislocations spreads the atoms apart and the volume rises by several percent
mechanical-018.explanation: The elastic volumetric strain is ΔV/V ≈ (1 − 2ν)ε, and Poisson's ratio of metals is about 0.3, so the volume increases slightly in tension (by 0.4 times the axial strain for ν = 0.30). The volume stays constant only for ν = 0.5, a value close to that of rubber. Plastic deformation, on the other hand, consists of atomic planes shifting by dislocation slip, so the volume hardly changes; this is why constant volume is assumed when calculating true stress and true strain. The volume change caused by the added dislocations is tiny, nowhere near several percent.

mechanical-019.question: In a tensile test of a ductile metal, once the tensile strength (the maximum engineering stress) is passed, the neck develops and the load falls. What happens to the true stress in the necked region during this stage?
choices: It falls in proportion to the load and is lowest just before fracture
It keeps rising until fracture because the area shrinks faster than the load falls
It peaks at the tensile strength and then stays constant until fracture
mechanical-019.explanation: After the tensile strength, the cross-sectional area in the neck decreases rapidly. The load falls, but the area falls faster, so the true stress σ_T = F/A keeps rising until fracture. The material continues to work-harden inside the neck; the load drops because the effect of the shrinking area outweighs the strengthening (the Considère condition). Reading the falling engineering stress as a weakening of the material is wrong, and the true stress does not stay constant either. Because the neck is under a triaxial stress state, an accurate flow stress requires a correction such as Bridgman's.

mechanical-020.question: A metal bar with a uniaxial tensile yield stress of 300 MPa is twisted (pure shear). According to the von Mises yield criterion, which is closest to the shear stress at which it yields?
choices: About 150 MPa
About 300 MPa
About 173 MPa
mechanical-020.explanation: Under the von Mises criterion the shear yield stress in pure shear is τy = σy/√3, so 300/1.732 ≈ 173 MPa. The principal stresses in pure shear are σ₁ = τ, σ₂ = 0 and σ₃ = −τ, and yielding occurs when the equivalent stress √{[(σ₁ − σ₂)² + (σ₂ − σ₃)² + (σ₃ − σ₁)²]/2} = √3τ reaches σy. About 150 MPa is the value from the Tresca criterion, which uses the maximum shear stress, τy = σy/2. About 300 MPa wrongly takes the shear yield stress to equal the tensile one. Torsion tests on ductile metals usually give values close to the von Mises prediction.

mechanical-021.question: In a Brinell hardness test, a ball indenter of diameter D = 10 mm is pressed in with F = 3000 kgf, leaving an indentation of diameter d = 4.0 mm. The Brinell hardness is the load F (kgf) divided by the surface area of the indentation (mm²), and this spherical-cap area is πDh, with depth h = [D − √(D² − d²)]/2. Which value is closest to the Brinell hardness?
choices: About 114
About 229
About 239
mechanical-021.explanation: The depth is h = [10 − √(100 − 16)]/2 = (10 − 9.165)/2 ≈ 0.417 mm, so the surface area is πDh = π × 10 × 0.417 ≈ 13.1 mm² and HB = 3000/13.1 ≈ 229. About 114 comes from forgetting to divide by 2 in the depth formula, which doubles the area. About 239 treats the indentation as a flat circle and divides by the projected area πd²/4 ≈ 12.6 mm²; that is a different quantity, the Meyer hardness. Because Brinell hardness uses the curved surface area, the gap from the projected-area value grows as the indentation gets deeper. The large indentation averages over coarse microstructures, but it is unsuitable for thin sheet or very hard materials.

mechanical-022.question: A metal bar 100 mm long is stretched uniformly, without necking, to 120 mm in a first pull and then to 150 mm in a second pull. Which value is closest to the sum of the true strains of the two pulls, each given by ε = ln(L/L₀) with L₀ the length at the start of that pull?
choices: About 0.41
About 0.45
About 0.50
mechanical-022.explanation: The first true strain is ln(120/100) = ln 1.20 ≈ 0.182 and the second is ln(150/120) = ln 1.25 ≈ 0.223, so the sum is about 0.405. This equals ln 1.50 ≈ 0.405 for stretching from 100 mm to 150 mm in one step, showing that true strains of successive stages can be added. About 0.45 adds the engineering strains 0.20 and 0.25, but engineering strains use a different reference length in each stage, so their sum does not give the overall engineering strain of 0.50. About 0.50 is that overall engineering strain itself, which is not a true strain. This is why the total deformation in repeated rolling or drawing passes is tracked with true strain.

mechanical-023.question: Tensile specimens that differ only in gauge length are machined from the same steel bar, and the elongation after fracture (the increase in gauge length after fracture divided by the original gauge length) is measured. What happens when the gauge length is made shorter?
choices: Elongation is a property of the material, so it stays the same within scatter whatever gauge length is used
The neck's extension spreads over a long gauge, so the longer the gauge length, the larger the elongation measured
Local extension concentrated in the neck makes up a larger share, so a shorter gauge gives a larger elongation
mechanical-023.explanation: The extension up to fracture consists of uniform elongation along the whole specimen and local elongation concentrated in the neck. The local extension hardly depends on gauge length and is set by the cross-section size, so the shorter the gauge length, the larger its share of the original length and the larger the measured elongation. Elongation after fracture therefore depends on specimen geometry and is not a material constant. Saying that longer gauges give larger values reverses the trend. Standards therefore compare results on matched geometries, such as proportional specimens whose gauge length scales with the square root of the cross-sectional area. Reduction of area at the fracture is also used as a ductility measure that does not depend on gauge length.

mechanical-024.question: When a stress-strain curve of a steel specimen is drawn using the crosshead displacement of the testing machine as the strain, the Young's modulus taken from the elastic slope often comes out much lower than the handbook value of about 200 GPa. What is the main reason?
choices: Heating during the test raises the specimen temperature, weakening atomic bonds and lowering the modulus itself
The displacement also includes elastic deflection of the frame and grips and slip in the grips, inflating the strain
Dislocations are already moving in the specimen, so plastic strain mixes into the elastic range and lowers the modulus
mechanical-024.explanation: Crosshead displacement includes not only the extension of the gauge section but also elastic deflection of the frame, load cell and grips, slip in the grips and deformation of the specimen shoulders. The strain is therefore overestimated, the slope comes out smaller, and the apparent modulus is low. For an accurate value, strain is measured directly with an extensometer on the gauge section, or the modulus is found dynamically from resonant frequency or ultrasonic wave speed. Temperature changes in the elastic range are tiny and do not shift the modulus appreciably. Small dislocation movements are not the main cause of such a large apparent drop either.

mechanical-025.question: Which statement about the Charpy impact test, in which a V-notched square bar is broken in a single blow by a swinging pendulum hammer, is correct?
choices: The energy used to break it comes from the loss in swing-up height; it is used to compare materials and locate the ductile-brittle transition
The energy used to break it gives the plane-strain fracture toughness K_IC directly, independent of crack length and without any conversion
The specimen is broken at the same strain rate as a slowly loaded tensile test, so the value equals the toughness from a tensile test
mechanical-025.explanation: In the Charpy test the raised hammer swings down and breaks the specimen, and the potential energy corresponding to how much lower the hammer swings up than its starting height is taken as the energy absorbed (J). The value depends on specimen size, notch shape and strain rate, so it cannot be used directly in strength calculations, but it is convenient for comparing materials or temperatures under the same conditions, and testing over a range of temperatures reveals the ductile-brittle transition temperature. K_IC is a separate quantity measured on fatigue-precracked specimens, and conversions from absorbed energy are only empirical estimates. The strain rate in an impact test is far higher than in a tensile test, and the absorbed energy is a different quantity from tensile toughness.

mechanical-026.question: In a test where a metal cylinder is compressed along its axis, the nominal stress (load divided by the original cross-sectional area) is compared with the true stress (load divided by the current area). Assuming uniform deformation at constant volume, which statement is correct?
choices: As in tension, the cross-section shrinks, so the magnitude of the true stress is larger than that of the nominal stress
With constant volume the cross-section does not change, so the true and nominal stresses are always equal
The cross-section grows, so the magnitude of the true stress is smaller than that of the nominal stress
mechanical-026.explanation: In compression the length decreases, and at constant volume the cross-section grows as A = A₀L₀/L. The true stress divides the load by this larger area, so its magnitude is smaller than that of the nominal stress. The relation is the same as in tension, σ = s(1 + e), except that e is negative. At a nominal strain of −0.20, for example, the true stress is 0.80 times the nominal stress in magnitude. The claim that the section shrinks as in tension gets the direction of deformation wrong. Even at constant volume, the area changes whenever the length changes. In real tests, friction at the end faces makes the middle bulge (barreling), so the deformation can be treated as uniform only at fairly small strains with the friction reduced by lubrication.

mechanical-027.question: Under plane stress, σx = 120 MPa, σy = 0 and the shear stress τxy = 80 MPa. Which is closest to the maximum principal stress σ₁ = (σx + σy)/2 + √[((σx − σy)/2)² + τxy²]?
choices: About 200 MPa
About 160 MPa
About 144 MPa
mechanical-027.explanation: (σx + σy)/2 = 60 MPa and √(60² + 80²) = √(3600 + 6400) = 100 MPa, so σ₁ = 60 + 100 = 160 MPa. The minimum principal stress is σ₂ = 60 − 100 = −40 MPa, and the maximum shear stress is half their difference, 100 MPa. About 200 MPa simply adds σx and τxy, and about 144 MPa is √(120² + 80²), which mixes up the center value (σx + σy)/2 with the radius calculation. No shear stress acts on the principal planes, and a brittle material tends to crack perpendicular to the largest principal stress when that stress reaches its strength. Yielding of ductile materials is judged by shear-related criteria such as the von Mises criterion.

mechanical-028.question: A rectangular bar of width b = 10 mm and thickness h = 4.0 mm is broken in three-point bending with a support span L = 40 mm by a central load F = 1.2 kN. If the central bending moment is M = FL/4 and the maximum surface bending stress is σ = 6M/(bh²), which is closest to the flexural strength?
choices: About 450 MPa
About 900 MPa
About 180 MPa
mechanical-028.explanation: M = 1200 N × 40 mm/4 = 12000 N·mm, and σ = 6 × 12000/(10 × 4.0²) = 72000/160 = 450 N/mm², or about 450 MPa (combined, σ = 3FL/(2bh²)). About 900 MPa takes the support reaction as F instead of F/2, giving M = F × L/2, and about 180 MPa swaps width and thickness to use 6M/(hb²). The thickness enters squared, so mixing them up makes a large difference. In three-point bending the maximum stress acts only on a very small region of the lower surface at mid-span, so for brittle materials such as ceramics a large flaw is less likely to lie there, and the value tends to exceed the tensile strength of the same material. Three-point values are therefore kept separate from four-point bending and tensile values.

mechanical-029.question: A block of metal is subjected only to a large pressure that is equal in all directions (hydrostatic pressure). What happens?
choices: Once the pressure exceeds the yield stress, the squeeze from all sides starts plastic flow and the volume decreases permanently
No shear stress arises, so it does not yield and only shrinks slightly according to its bulk modulus
The von Mises equivalent stress is √3 times the pressure, so the block yields when the pressure reaches about 58% of the yield stress
mechanical-029.explanation: Plastic deformation of metals is shear deformation by dislocation slip, so yielding is governed by the shear-related part of the stress (the deviatoric stress) and hardly depends on the hydrostatic component, which is equal in all directions. Pure hydrostatic pressure produces no shear stress on any plane, so the von Mises equivalent stress is zero and no yielding occurs. The volume shrinks elastically by ΔV/V = −p/K according to the bulk modulus K and recovers when the pressure is removed. Plastic deformation does not reduce the volume permanently. Superimposing hydrostatic pressure on tension or other deformation does, however, suppress the growth of small internal cavities (voids) and increase the ductility before fracture, which is exploited in processes such as extrusion.

mechanical-030.question: Which statement about Poisson's ratio is correct? Assume isotropic materials.
choices: Rubber stretches so much that its Poisson's ratio exceeds 1, while soft cork is close to 0.5 and spreads out widely when pushed
Poisson's ratio does not depend on the type of atomic bonding, so rubber, metals and cork all have nearly the same value of about 0.3
Rubber is close to 0.5 and hardly changes volume, while cork is close to 0 and barely spreads sideways when pushed in
mechanical-030.explanation: Poisson's ratio ν is the ratio of lateral contraction to axial strain. At small strains the volume change is proportional to (1 − 2ν), so at ν = 0.5 the volume does not change, and for isotropic materials this is the upper limit. The claim that ν exceeds 1 is therefore wrong. Rubber resists changes in volume but changes shape easily, so ν is almost 0.5. Cork shortens as the walls of its hollow cells fold, so ν is almost 0; it hardly bulges sideways when pushed into the neck of a bottle, which makes it a good stopper. Most metals are around 0.3. As this shows, ν varies widely with the type of bonding and the internal structure.
